newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate said set to approve Cohen quickly.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate said set to approve Cohen quickly.

text.p: Republican William Cohen of Maine, President's Clinton's nominee to become Defence Secretary, could be confirmed by the Senate and sworn in as soon as Thursday, Pentagon and Senate officials said Tuesday.

Cohen, who retired from the Senate this month, testifies to the Armed Services Committee Wednesday in his confirmation hearing to replace William Perry. He is expected to get quick committee endorsement as the first Republican in Clinton's Cabinet.
"The Senate is hoping to be able to confirm him on Thursday," Pentagon spokesman Ken Bacon said Wednesday. "We believe that Senator Cohen should become Secretary Cohen on Thursday or Friday."

Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott told reporters he would schedule Senate votes Wednesday to confirm Madeleine Albright to be secretary of state and Thursday to confirm Cohen to be secretary of defence, if Cohen's confirmation hearing is completed by then.

Bacon said Cohen, a 24-year veteran of Congress and an expert on defence and intelligence issues, will devote his early weeks at the Defence Department to the fiscal 1998 defence budget and to a major Quadrennial Defence Review of U.S. military policy.
After presenting the budget to Congress in hearings early next month, Cohen, 56, is likely to begin travelling to visit U.S. troops and foreign leaders, Bacon said.

"There have been a series of requests and invitations which he has not acted on finally but will when he becomes secretary," Bacon said. "He will have to sit down and make out a schedule of people coming here to visit him as well as people he will visit and when."
Cohen is a strong supporter of NATO and of close U.S. military ties with Asia and with Europe including Russia and other emerging democracies in the former Soviet bloc.

Defence experts say there will be little or no change in policy under Cohen, considered a moderate in a Republican party increasingly dominated by conservatives. Clinton chose Cohen for the job to emphasise his second-term promise to work closely with the Republican-controlled Congress.
Some members of Congress charge that defence budget cuts in recent years have left the military close to being the "hollow force" it became in the post-Vietnam War drawdown.

Cohen was vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee from 1987 to 1991 and of the joint congressional committee that investigated the Iran-Contra affair involving President Ronald Reagan's administration in the late 1980s.
He has published two books of poetry, three non-fiction books and three spy or mystery novels.

Despite his years of legislating on defence, intelligence and foreign affairs policy he has no experience conducting policy or running a federal agency. He will also follow one of the most popular and effective American defence secretaries.

Perry, 69, was a foreign and defence policy leader in the Clinton Cabinet and travelled 650,000 miles in three years on the job, establishing personal ties with defence ministers around the world and wooing former Soviet allies to closer ties with NATO.
